papers.title: Enabling Privacy-Preserving Natural Language Access to Industrial Smart Meter Data
papers.abstract: Energy management officers and grid operators increasingly rely on smart meter data for anomaly detection, performance monitoring, and strategic decision-making. However, extracting actionable insights from large-scale, heterogeneous telemetry databases requires advanced SQL and data engineering expertise, creating a critical bottleneck for non-technical personnel. Furthermore, the strict data privacy regulations and security constraints inherent to critical energy infrastructure often prohibit the routing of sensitive consumer data through cloud-based Large Language Models (LLMs). To address these challenges, we present OpenMeter, a schema-agnostic Multi-Agent System (MAS) designed to translate natural language queries into executable code and human-readable insights. This architecture lowers the technical barrier for day-to-day utility operations by empowering non-expert personnel to interact with complex databases through intuitive natural language dialogue, transforming raw telemetry into a highly valuable tool for routine grid workflows and strategic decisions. Multi-scenario ablation studies over this environment demonstrate that full multi-agent orchestration shows its largest observed accuracy gains on resource-constrained local hardware (+6.1 pp EX-R over the strongest single-agent configuration); at frontier scale, individual components retain value but should be enabled selectively, indicating that the cost of full orchestration is justified specifically where privacy demands local execution.
papers.ranking_reason: This paper shows how non-technical workers can safely query complex energy databases using natural language.
papers.explanation: This paper introduces a system that lets users ask questions in plain English instead of writing complex database code. It runs locally on your computer to keep sensitive data private without using cloud servers.
papers.why_it_matters: It shows you how to build privacy-friendly AI tools that connect human questions to structured databases securely.

project_idea.title: Local SQL Chatbot
project_idea.description: Write a Python script using SQLite and a local LLM [large language model, an AI that understands text] to answer questions about a small energy dataset. Translate plain text questions into SQL queries locally.
project_idea.no_code_version: Use Google Sheets with an OpenAI or local plugin to let users query spreadsheet rows using natural language prompts.

papers.title: RAG-Enhanced LLMs for Interactive Explainability in Clinical Decision Support Systems
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in high-risks decision-making systems across domains such as healthcare, finance, and the judicial system. As reliance on predictive models grows, so does the demand for Explainable AI (XAI) to ensure transparency, trust, and interpretability. However, existing XAI approaches often fail to present explanations in a format accessible to domain experts, limiting their practical utility. Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently emerged as a bridge between complex models and end-users, offering natural language explanations. Yet, their use introduces new risks, including hallucinated outputs and lack of source traceability. To address these challenges, we propose a Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) that not only combines standard predictive models with XAI techniques but also incorporates a Retrieval-Augmented Generation module as an interactive enhancer. This module grounds explanations in verified medical knowledge, reformulates technical outputs into a human-like format, and enables users-such as clinicians-to actively query the system. By fostering an interactive, human-in-the-loop environment, our approach empowers domain experts to explore model decisions, contextualize explanations, and build trust in AI-assisted diagnostics. The study concludes with preliminary experiments validating the proposed methodology.
papers.ranking_reason: This paper explains how AI can provide clear natural language explanations for high-risk decisions.
papers.explanation: The authors built a clinical support system that pairs predictive AI models with RAG [retrieval-augmented generation, a technique that fetches facts from documents before the AI generates an answer]. This grounds the AI's explanations in verified medical knowledge so doctors can trust the output.
papers.why_it_matters: It teaches you how to make AI predictions trustworthy and explainable by linking them to real source documents.

project_idea.title: Explainable Symptom Checker
project_idea.description: Build a simple RAG pipeline that searches through medical guideline documents and explains disease predictions in plain language. Include source citations in every output.
project_idea.no_code_version: Use an n8n workflow that takes a user query, searches a Google Drive folder of medical text files, and passes them to an LLM to generate an explained response.

papers.title: Goals as a Representational Layer for Human-AI Collaboration
papers.abstract: Goals are central to how people, teams, and organizations structure their work. Yet, while generative artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly operate across a worker's context, information about why a person is pursuing a task, beyond local prompts and interactions, is typically missing. We argue that goals should become an explicit representational layer mediating interactions among people, AI systems, and organizations. Because human goals are hierarchical, partially latent, and dynamically evolving, such a layer must be multidimensional, both grounded in human articulation and inferred from available evidence, and continuously updated. A goal layer could connect immediate requests to broader outcomes, improve the organization and retrieval of relevant context, support reflection and coordination, and provide a foundation for training, aligning, and evaluating AI systems in terms of human-centered outcomes. We highlight these opportunities while identifying open challenges involving goal inference, socio-cognitive frictions, alignment, privacy, and governance.
papers.ranking_reason: This paper explores how human goals can serve as a bridge to improve collaboration with AI systems.
papers.explanation: This paper argues that AI systems need to understand human goals, rather than just following local prompts. A goal layer helps the AI track what you ultimately want to achieve across multiple tasks.
papers.why_it_matters: It introduces a helpful way to design AI assistants that remember your long-term objectives instead of treating every prompt as brand new.

project_idea.title: Goal Tracker Assistant
project_idea.description: Build a chatbot that stores user goals in a JSON file and checks if new tasks align with those goals. Print a reminder of the main objective before every response.
project_idea.no_code_version: Create a Notion database for your goals and use Make to automatically append your active project goal to every prompt you send to an AI module.

papers.title: What to Delegate, What to Preserve: Human Preferences for Agentic AI Across Everyday Life and Work
papers.abstract: AI agents can execute multi-step tasks on users' behalf, yet the boundaries of acceptable delegation remain unclear. We report a scenario-based survey of 289 U.S. adults with prior AI experience covering 45 use cases across nine life domains. Each respondent evaluated one scenario per domain, producing repeated measures of automation preference, trust, collaboration, AI leadership, privacy concern, and willingness to pay. Automation preferences varied substantially across domains. Generalized estimating equation models showed that greater trust in the AI agent, desired AI leadership, prior task-specific AI use, and anticipated financial savings were associated with greater automation preference. In contrast, concerns that automation would reduce personal fulfillment predicted lower automation preference. Open-ended responses further revealed a preference for bounded autonomy, with participants often favoring substantial AI execution while retaining human involvement, oversight, or final authority. We argue that delegation is best understood as a configuration of execution, collaboration, leadership, and authority.
papers.ranking_reason: This paper investigates what tasks everyday people are actually willing to delegate to autonomous AI agents.
papers.explanation: This paper surveyed people to find out which tasks they are willing to delegate to autonomous AI agents. Most people want the AI to do the heavy lifting, but they still want to keep final authority and oversight.
papers.why_it_matters: It helps you design AI applications that respect user boundaries and maintain the right balance of human control.

project_idea.title: Approval-Required Task Agent
project_idea.description: Code a multi-step Python agent that drafts emails or file updates, but pauses execution to ask the user for explicit approval before making any changes.
project_idea.no_code_version: Build an n8n workflow that generates a draft response using AI and sends a Slack approval button to your phone before posting it live.

papers.title: Decision Context: Persistent Behavioral Learning for AI Agents
papers.abstract: LLM agents do not learn from corrections across sessions. A user fixes the same mistake at the start of every conversation. Existing agent memory systems primarily handle facts, such as preferences, entities, and conversational history, rather than procedural knowledge. We present Forge Decision Context (forge_dc), a system that captures behavioral signals from human corrections and self-assessed tool-call failures, compiles them into imperative RULE directives, and injects them at the decision points where they apply. We evaluate forge_dc alongside four predecessor approaches on DC-Bench, a new benchmark of 71 scenarios across nine behavioral dimensions, built from real executed agent traces in a deterministic mocked-tool environment. forge_dc reaches 95% compliance, up from 55% with naive retrieval, while injecting approximately 10 times fewer tokens per query. Across the five-stage progression, the strongest systems represent behavioral memory as explicit directives and deliver it at the decision points where it applies. The results identify representation, activation, and placement as central design choices for persistent behavioral learning.
papers.ranking_reason: This paper presents a system that allows AI agents to learn from your corrections so you do not repeat them.
papers.explanation: The authors created a memory system that captures human corrections when an AI makes a mistake. It turns those corrections into explicit rules and injects them back into the prompt so the AI does not repeat the same error.
papers.why_it_matters: It solves the frustrating problem where AI agents forget your feedback and make the exact same mistake in the next session.

project_idea.title: Self-Correcting Chatbot Memory
project_idea.description: Write a Python script that detects when a user corrects the AI, saves that correction as a rule in a text file, and adds it to the system prompt for future turns.
project_idea.no_code_version: Set up an Airtable base to log user corrections and use Make to dynamically prepend those logged corrections to your chatbot's system instructions.
